summary.title: Hello World Auth App (React + Spring Boot)
summary.description:
Threat model for the secured username/password login application specified in prd/assessment-prd.md: a React SPA on its own origin against a Spring Boot REST API, authenticated by a server-side session carried in an HttpOnly cookie.

Assets protected: account credentials (BCrypt hashes), session cookies, password-reset tokens, user email addresses, and the ADMIN privilege itself.

Trust boundaries: (1) browser to backend, crossing origins with credentials, guarded by CORS plus cookie-based CSRF; (2) unauthenticated to authenticated, at the form-login filter; (3) USER to ADMIN, at the /api/admin/** URL matcher; (4) application to data stores and log sinks.

External dependencies: none at runtime beyond H2 (dev). Email delivery is a stub that logs. JWT, MFA, real SMTP, containerisation and local HTTPS are out of scope per the PRD.

Methodology: STRIDE per element across a Level 0 context diagram and three Level 1 decompositions, plus a LINDDUN pass because the system stores email addresses. Statuses are Open, Mitigated or Not applicable; Mitigated entries name the control and, where one exists, the test that asserts it.

Companion report: docs/threat-model/hello-world-auth-app-threat-model.md

data.name: Visitor / User
data.description: Unauthenticated visitor or authenticated USER, driving a browser on a separate origin (localhost:3000).

threats.title: TM-22: Registration conflict responses reveal whether an account exists
threats.description:
POST /api/auth/register answers 409 with a distinct message for a taken username vs a taken email, so an unauthenticated caller can enumerate registered usernames and email addresses. The PRD scopes enumeration resistance to login and password reset only, so this is in-spec, but it is still a live disclosure channel and it undermines the enumeration guarantee the other two endpoints provide.

Evidence: backend/.../auth/RegistrationService.java:45-52
threats.mitigation: Accept as a documented deviation, or return a uniform 202/200 for registration and deliver the 'account already exists' signal out of band by email. Record the decision as an ADR either way.

threats.title: Credential-stuffing and brute force against login
threats.description: An attacker replays breached or guessed username/password pairs against POST /api/auth/login.
threats.mitigation: Mitigated by per-account lockout (5 failures → 15 min, LockoutPolicy:14-18) and per-IP throttling (10 failures / 15 min, IpLoginThrottle:27-28), plus BCrypt work factor on every attempt. Residual weaknesses in both controls are tracked separately as TM-08, TM-09 and TM-10.

threats.title: Username enumeration via login responses
threats.description: Differing responses for an unknown username vs a wrong password would let an attacker harvest valid usernames before spending guesses on passwords.
threats.mitigation: Mitigated: LoginFailureHandler always returns 401 with the single generic message 'Invalid username or password'. Asserted by LoginLogoutHelloTest.unknownUsernameReturnsIdenticalGenericErrorAsWrongPassword.

data.name: Admin
data.description: Authenticated account holder with role ADMIN; can list, enable/disable, re-role and delete other accounts.

threats.title: TM-07: Dev profile ships a fixed, publicly documented admin password
threats.description:
The dev profile defaults the bootstrap admin to admin / password1234, and the same credentials are printed in README.md and rendered in the SPA's dev login form. The dev profile is also the profile every backend test runs under, and it is the only profile with a working datasource — so it is the profile anyone actually starts the app with. Any dev/demo instance reachable beyond localhost is a trivial full-admin takeover.

Evidence: backend/src/main/resources/application.yml:58-61; README.md:82; frontend/src/LoginForm.tsx:45, 66
threats.mitigation: Keep the mandatory no-default binding of the base profile as the only supported path. Remove the dev defaults and require APP_ADMIN_USERNAME/APP_ADMIN_PASSWORD even in dev (a .env.example or a generated random password logged once at startup), force a password change on first admin login, and bind the dev server to 127.0.0.1.

data.name: React SPA (Vite)
data.description: React 18 single-page app on its own origin. Holds auth state in memory only; reads the XSRF-TOKEN cookie and echoes it as X-XSRF-TOKEN on every mutating call.

threats.title: TM-13: No Content-Security-Policy, and the CSRF token is readable by script
threats.description:
The backend sets no CSP, Referrer-Policy or Permissions-Policy header — the only header customisation is frameOptions().sameOrigin(), which loosens rather than tightens the defaults. Because CSRF uses CookieCsrfTokenRepository.withHttpOnlyFalse(), the token is deliberately script-readable, so any XSS foothold in the SPA reads the token and defeats CSRF protection wholesale while riding the HttpOnly session cookie. Today the SPA has no XSS sink (no dangerouslySetInnerHTML, no innerHTML, no eval, all server data rendered as JSX text), so this is a defence-in-depth gap rather than an exploitable chain.

Evidence: backend/.../config/SecurityConfig.java:85, 108-110; frontend/src/api/client.ts:10-14
threats.mitigation: Add a restrictive CSP (default-src 'self', no unsafe-inline for scripts) plus Referrer-Policy: no-referrer and X-Content-Type-Options via Spring Security's headers DSL. Keep the no-XSS-sink discipline enforced by lint rather than by convention.

threats.title: TM-26: Production bundle falls back to http://localhost:8080
threats.description:
The API base URL is import.meta.env.VITE_API_BASE_URL ?? 'http://localhost:8080'. A build made without VITE_API_BASE_URL set silently ships a bundle that points every request at the visitor's own machine — a broken deployment, and on a developer machine a cross-origin request to whatever is listening on 8080.

Evidence: frontend/src/api/client.ts:1
threats.mitigation: Fail the build when VITE_API_BASE_URL is unset for production (assert in vite.config.ts or a prebuild step) instead of falling back to a localhost default.

threats.title: Session token theft from client-side storage
threats.description: Tokens kept in localStorage/sessionStorage are readable by any injected script.
threats.mitigation: Mitigated by design: there is no client-side token. Auth rests on an HttpOnly SESSION cookie and the SPA keeps only the non-secret {username, role} in a React useState. Grep confirms no localStorage, sessionStorage or IndexedDB use anywhere in frontend/src.

threats.title: Stored/reflected XSS through rendered server data
threats.description: Usernames, emails and error messages returned by the API are attacker-influenced and rendered back into the admin list and greeting views.
threats.mitigation: Mitigated: every value renders as a JSX text node, so React escapes it. No dangerouslySetInnerHTML, innerHTML, eval or direct DOM writes exist in the codebase. The reset token read from window.location.search is only ever used as a form value.

data.name: Spring Boot REST API
data.description: Spring Boot 3.5.16 / Java 21. Single SecurityFilterChain: CORS, IP throttle, CSRF, form login, URL-based authorization, REST exception handling.

threats.title: TM-06: CORS allow-list is environment-driven; one bad value collapses origin isolation
threats.description:
allowedOrigins comes from APP_CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS and allowCredentials is true, with allowedHeaders '*'. The strict origin list is the load-bearing control: if that variable is ever set to an attacker-reachable origin (or widened during debugging), any page on that origin can read the XSRF-TOKEN cookie's echo path, make credentialed calls with the victim's SESSION cookie, and read the responses. There is no startup validation rejecting wildcards or non-HTTPS origins.

Evidence: backend/.../config/CorsConfig.java:29, 37-42
threats.mitigation: Validate the configured origins at startup: reject '*', reject null/empty, and require https:// outside dev. Fail fast rather than booting with a permissive list. Add an integration test asserting a disallowed Origin is refused.

threats.title: TM-14: Admin authorization depends on a single URL matcher, with no method-level backstop
threats.description:
requestMatchers("/api/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN") is the only thing standing between a USER and every admin capability. @EnableMethodSecurity is absent and no @PreAuthorize appears anywhere, and the controller deliberately does not re-check the role. Any future admin-capable handler mounted outside the /api/admin/** prefix, or a matcher-ordering mistake, is unguarded with no second line of defence.

Evidence: backend/.../config/SecurityConfig.java:122-132; backend/.../admin/AdminUserController.java:21-28
threats.mitigation: Enable method security and annotate the admin service (not just the controller) with @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')"), so authorization travels with the capability rather than with the URL.

threats.title: TM-11: Rate limiting covers only POST /api/auth/login
threats.description:
IpThrottleFilter matches POST /api/auth/login and nothing else. Registration, both password-reset endpoints, and every admin mutation are unthrottled. Registration and reset-confirm each run a BCrypt hash, so an unauthenticated caller can spend ~100ms of server CPU per request at negligible cost to themselves and pollute the users table at will.

Evidence: backend/.../auth/IpThrottleFilter.java:44-45
threats.mitigation: Apply a shared rate-limit filter (or Bucket4j/Resilience4j) to all unauthenticated write endpoints, keyed on client IP and, for reset, on the target email. Add a CAPTCHA or proof-of-work on registration if it is ever public.

threats.title: TM-12: No request body or connection limits, in front of deliberately expensive work
threats.description:
application.yml configures no max-http-form-post-size, no max-http-request-header-size, no multipart limits and no Tomcat thread/connection caps. Spring Boot applies no default cap to JSON request bodies, so an unauthenticated client can post an arbitrarily large body to /api/auth/register and force the server to buffer and Jackson-parse it before validation rejects it.

Evidence: backend/src/main/resources/application.yml (no server.tomcat.* or size limits present)
threats.mitigation: Set server.tomcat.max-http-form-post-size and max-swallow-size, add a @Size cap on every string field in the request DTOs (username, email, password, token), and cap Tomcat threads/connections.

threats.title: TM-24: No catch-all exception handler, so unmapped failures answer in a different shape
threats.description:
Three package-scoped @RestControllerAdvice classes cover auth, admin and password-reset and all emit {message, details[]}. Anything they do not map — including any failure in /api/hello, /api/health or /api/csrf — falls through to Boot's default /error handling, which emits a different JSON shape that the SPA's parseErrorResponse cannot read. Boot defaults suppress stack traces, so this is a robustness and consistency problem rather than a leak today, but it is one property change (server.error.include-stacktrace) away from being one.

Evidence: backend/.../auth/AuthExceptionHandler.java; admin/AdminExceptionHandler.java; passwordreset/PasswordResetExceptionHandler.java
threats.mitigation: Add a global @RestControllerAdvice handling Exception → 500 {message, details} with no internals, and pin server.error.include-stacktrace=never and include-message=never explicitly.

threats.title: TM-28: No dependency vulnerability scanning or SBOM in the build
threats.description:
pom.xml carries only spring-boot-maven-plugin — no OWASP dependency-check, no CycloneDX SBOM plugin, and the frontend has no audit step in its scripts. A vulnerable transitive dependency would reach a deployment unnoticed, and there is no inventory to answer 'are we affected' against a new CVE.

Evidence: backend/pom.xml; frontend/package.json
threats.mitigation: Add cyclonedx-maven-plugin and dependency-check (or Dependabot/Renovate plus `npm audit --audit-level=high` in CI) and fail the build on high severity findings.

threats.title: Cross-site request forgery against cookie-authenticated mutations
threats.description: Auth rests on an ambient session cookie, so any hostile page could otherwise drive state-changing requests as the victim.
threats.mitigation: Mitigated: CSRF is enabled for every state-changing endpoint via CookieCsrfTokenRepository plus CsrfTokenRequestAttributeHandler; the SPA echoes the cookie as X-XSRF-TOKEN, and SameSite=Lax blocks the cookie on cross-site POSTs as a second layer. Note no test asserts a missing token is rejected — see the report's testing gaps.

threats.title: SQL injection via request parameters
threats.description: Classic injection into persistence queries.
threats.mitigation: Not applicable: every repository method is a Spring Data derived query. There is no @Query, no native SQL and no string-concatenated SQL anywhere in the codebase, so no injectable surface exists.

threats.title: Client-supplied role or identity trusted for authorization
threats.description: If the server read the acting user's id or role from the request body, a USER could self-promote or act as another admin.
threats.mitigation: Mitigated: role comes from the authenticated principal via Spring Security, and the acting admin id comes from @AuthenticationPrincipal UserPrincipal, never from the payload. The SPA's role check is cosmetic only; AdminUserControllerTest asserts a USER receives 403 on every admin mutation.

data.name: H2 web console (/h2-console/**)
data.description: H2's own servlet, registered when spring.h2.console.enabled=true (dev profile).

threats.title: TM-01: The H2 console's permitAll and CSRF exemption are not profile-gated
threats.description:
SecurityConfig unconditionally grants permitAll to /h2-console/**, exempts it from CSRF, and weakens frame-options to sameOrigin for the entire application. The inline comments argue this is safe because the servlet only exists when spring.h2.console.enabled=true — but the rules themselves ship in every profile, the H2 jar sits on the runtime classpath of every build, and the datasource credentials are sa with a blank password. Anyone who can reach the port in a dev or demo deployment gets unauthenticated full SQL read/write: dump password hashes, mint themselves an ADMIN row, or drop the schema. The global frame-options relaxation also weakens clickjacking protection on the real API for no benefit.

Evidence: backend/.../config/SecurityConfig.java:104, 108-110, 130; backend/src/main/resources/application.yml:41-50
threats.mitigation: Move these rules behind @Profile("dev") (a separate dev-only SecurityFilterChain bean), scope frameOptions().sameOrigin() to /h2-console/** only, set spring.h2.console.settings.web-allow-others=false, and move the h2 dependency to <scope>test</scope> once a real datasource exists.

data.name: H2 in-memory database
data.description: jdbc:h2:mem:hello-world-auth-app, user sa, blank password, ddl-auto: update. Tables: users, password_reset_tokens. Dev profile only — no other datasource is configured.

threats.title: TM-19: No non-dev datasource, no migrations, and the dev one has no password
threats.description:
The only datasource in the repo is the dev H2 in-memory instance: user sa, blank password, ddl-auto: update, DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1. There is no application-prod.yml, no Flyway or Liquibase, and no schema scripts, so the app as committed cannot start outside dev and 'portable to Postgres/MySQL later' is aspirational. ddl-auto: update also means Hibernate mutates the schema at boot from entity state — acceptable in dev, unsafe anywhere data matters. All credential material lives in a store with no authentication in front of it.

Evidence: backend/src/main/resources/application.yml:35-50
threats.mitigation: Add a prod profile with an external datasource, credentials from the environment or a secret manager, ddl-auto: validate, and Flyway-managed migrations. Give the dev H2 instance a password even in dev.

threats.title: TM-20: BCrypt strength is implicit and password length is uncapped
threats.description:
new BCryptPasswordEncoder() takes the default strength of 10, with no configuration hook to raise it as hardware improves. Separately, PasswordPolicy enforces a 12-character minimum and nothing else — no maximum — and BCrypt silently truncates input beyond 72 bytes, so the tail of a long passphrase contributes nothing to the hash while the user believes it does.

Evidence: backend/.../config/SecurityConfig.java:49-51; backend/.../auth/PasswordPolicy.java:13-17
threats.mitigation: Construct the encoder with an explicit, configurable strength (≥12) and add a documented maximum password length of 72 bytes to PasswordPolicy so truncation can never happen silently. Consider a breached-password check against the Pwned Passwords range API.

threats.title: Password recovery from stolen hashes
threats.description: An attacker who reads the users table attempts offline recovery of plaintext passwords.
threats.mitigation: Mitigated: passwords are stored only as BCrypt hashes (per-hash salt, adaptive work factor), never plaintext or reversible encoding. AdminBootstrapRunnerTest asserts even the seeded admin password is hashed. Residual work-factor concern tracked as TM-20.

threats.title: Password hashes leaked through the admin API
threats.description: An over-broad admin listing response could serialise the whole User entity including password_hash.
threats.mitigation: Mitigated: /api/admin/users returns a purpose-built UserSummaryResponse projection (id, username, email, role, enabled, createdAt). AdminUserControllerTest explicitly asserts no password hash appears in the response body.

threats.title: Total data loss on restart
threats.description: An in-memory database discards every account on process exit.
threats.mitigation: Accepted for a demo/reference build and superseded by TM-19: the fix is a real persistent datasource, tracked there. No separate remediation.

data.name: HTTP session store + SessionRegistry (in-memory)
data.description: Plain Tomcat in-process HttpSession (no Spring Session dependency) plus SessionRegistryImpl for 'log out everywhere'.

threats.title: TM-16: No session timeout or absolute lifetime is configured
threats.description:
application.yml sets cookie attributes but never server.servlet.session.timeout, so idle expiry is whatever the container defaults to (30 minutes for Tomcat) — an implicit value nobody chose. There is also no absolute session lifetime: a session kept warm by periodic activity lives indefinitely, so a stolen cookie stays valid for as long as the attacker keeps using it.

Evidence: backend/src/main/resources/application.yml (no server.servlet.session.timeout)
threats.mitigation: Set server.servlet.session.timeout explicitly (e.g. 15–30 minutes) and enforce an absolute cap by recording session creation time and rejecting sessions past a maximum age.

threats.title: TM-25: Session state and throttle state are process-local
threats.description:
Sessions, SessionRegistryImpl and the IP-throttle map all live in the JVM heap of a single instance. Running two instances behind a load balancer breaks session continuity, makes 'invalidate all sessions on password reset' cover only the instance that served the reset, and lets an attacker get N times the throttle budget by spreading attempts across instances. This is documented in IpLoginThrottle's Javadoc as a known limitation.

Evidence: backend/.../auth/IpLoginThrottle.java:19-23, 33; backend/.../config/SecurityConfig.java:60-62
threats.mitigation: Move sessions to Spring Session (JDBC or Redis) and the throttle counters to the same shared store before running more than one instance. Until then, document single-instance deployment as a constraint.

threats.title: Session fixation
threats.description: An attacker who plants a known session identifier before login would own the session once the victim authenticates.
threats.mitigation: Mitigated by Spring Security's default ChangeSessionIdAuthenticationStrategy, which rotates the session ID on successful authentication. Relied on rather than overridden — note no test asserts the rotation.

threats.title: Session replay after logout
threats.description: A cookie captured before logout is replayed afterwards.
threats.mitigation: Mitigated: logout invalidates the server-side session and deletes the SESSION cookie. LoginLogoutHelloTest.logoutInvalidatesSessionAndReplayedCookieIsRejected asserts the replayed cookie is rejected as unauthenticated.

data.name: Application logs (stdout)
data.description: SLF4J over Boot's default console appender. No logback-spring.xml, no JSON encoder, no MDC, no file or retention configuration.

threats.title: TM-02: The password-reset link, including the live plaintext token, is written to the log
threats.description:
The stubbed EmailService logs the complete reset link at INFO. That link contains the plaintext, currently-valid, single-use reset token. Anyone with log read access — an operator, a log aggregator, a CI job tailing output, a support engineer with a screenshot — can take over any account that has requested a reset, within the 30-minute window. This is the sharpest finding in the model: it converts read access to logs into account takeover, and it directly contradicts the PRD's 'never log secrets' requirement even though the letter of that requirement only names passwords.

Evidence: backend/.../passwordreset/EmailService.java:16-18
threats.mitigation: Log only a correlation id and the target user id — never the token or the assembled link. When the real EmailService lands, keep the token out of every log statement on that path and add a test asserting the token value never appears in captured log output.

threats.title: TM-15: Log injection via the unvalidated username field
threats.description:
LoginFailureHandler logs the raw username request parameter, and the login endpoint applies no validation at all to it — no length bound, no character restriction. RegistrationRequest constrains username only with @Size(3, 64) and no @Pattern, so control characters and CRLF pass validation and reach the registration log line too. An attacker can embed newlines to forge convincing log entries, corrupting exactly the audit trail the PRD relies on for accountability, and can break a downstream log parser.

Evidence: backend/.../auth/LoginFailureHandler.java:64, 77; backend/.../auth/RegistrationRequest.java:13-24; backend/.../auth/RegistrationService.java:58
threats.mitigation: Add @Pattern(regexp = "[A-Za-z0-9._-]+") to the username field, and sanitise or encode any user-controlled value before logging (strip CR/LF, cap length). Emit logs as JSON so field boundaries are structural rather than textual.

threats.title: TM-27: Audit lines are unstructured and uncorrelated, with no retention or integrity story
threats.description:
The PRD asks for structured audit log lines covering login success/failure, lockout, reset request/completion and admin mutations. All those events are logged, but as ad-hoc key=value text through Boot's default console pattern — no JSON encoder, no MDC or correlation id to tie a request chain together, no request source recorded on admin actions, and no retention, shipping or tamper-protection configuration. Reconstructing 'who disabled this account, from where, in which request' is guesswork.

Evidence: backend/src/main/resources (no logback-spring.xml); prd/assessment-prd.md:122
threats.mitigation: Add logback-spring.xml with a JSON encoder, populate MDC with a per-request correlation id and the authenticated principal via a filter, include the client IP on admin mutations, and ship logs to an append-only sink with a defined retention period.

threats.title: Plaintext passwords written to logs
threats.description: Logging a request payload or an authentication exception can capture the submitted password.
threats.mitigation: Mitigated: no log statement references a password field, and the exception handlers deliberately log messages without payloads. Verified by reading every log call site in the backend.

data.name: EmailService (stub)
data.description: Stub implementation. Logs the reset link instead of sending mail; real SMTP is explicitly out of scope.

threats.title: TM-03: The reset token travels in a URL query parameter
threats.description:
The reset link is built as frontendBaseUrl + "/?token=" + plaintextToken, so the token is transmitted as a query parameter.

Partially mitigated on the client: App.tsx samples the token into React state and then erases it from the address bar with history.replaceState on mount, which closes the browser-history, bookmark and shared-link vectors. The app also loads no external subresources at all (index.html pulls only the local module), so there is no third-party Referer leak today.

Residual exposure: replaceState runs in the browser after the request has already been sent, so the token still appears in the access logs of whatever serves the frontend (the Vite dev server, or a CDN/reverse proxy in production) and in any intermediary that records URLs. That is outside this application's control and cannot be fixed client-side. The absence of a Referrer-Policy header also means the protection against third-party leakage rests entirely on nobody ever adding an external script, font or image to the reset page.

Evidence: backend/.../passwordreset/PasswordResetService.java:90; mitigating code at frontend/src/App.tsx:18-20, 39-42
threats.mitigation: Deliver the token in the URL fragment (#token=...) instead of the query string. Fragments are never sent to a server, which closes the access-log vector that replaceState cannot reach; the SPA then reads location.hash and clears it exactly as it clears the query string today. Set Referrer-Policy: no-referrer regardless, so the no-subresources property does not have to hold forever.

threats.title: TM-05: No transport security is enforced anywhere in the application
threats.description:
The filter chain has no requiresChannel()/HTTPS redirect, HSTS is only emitted by Spring Security's default when a request already arrives over HTTPS, and the dev profile overrides the session cookie to secure: false. Local dev over HTTP is an accepted, documented gap in the PRD — but nothing in the code or config prevents the same build from serving plaintext outside dev, and in that case the SESSION cookie, submitted passwords and reset tokens all cross the network in the clear and are trivially sniffed or MITM'd. There is also no forward-headers-strategy, so behind a TLS-terminating proxy the app cannot even tell whether the original request was secure.

Evidence: backend/.../config/SecurityConfig.java:108-110; backend/src/main/resources/application.yml:5-15, 52-56
threats.mitigation: Add requiresChannel().anyRequest().requiresSecure() and an explicit HSTS policy (long max-age, includeSubDomains) outside dev, set server.forward-headers-strategy=framework so proxy headers are honoured, and keep secure: false confined to the dev profile as it is today.

threats.title: TM-21: CSRF tokens are not masked against BREACH
threats.description:
The chain wires CsrfTokenRequestAttributeHandler rather than the XorCsrfTokenRequestAttributeHandler that Spring Security defaults to. The Xor handler randomises the token per response specifically to frustrate BREACH-style compression side-channel extraction; using the plain handler gives that up. Exploitation needs response compression plus an attacker-observable network position, so the practical risk here is small.

Evidence: backend/.../config/SecurityConfig.java:86, 99
threats.mitigation: Switch to XorCsrfTokenRequestAttributeHandler with setCsrfRequestAttributeName(null), the documented pattern for SPAs that read the token from a cookie.

threats.title: TM-19b: Database connections are unauthenticated and unencrypted
threats.description:
The dev datasource is in-process H2 with a blank sa password, so there is nothing on the wire to protect today. The finding is forward-looking: no TLS or credential handling pattern exists for the Postgres/MySQL migration the PRD anticipates, so the first real deployment starts from zero.

Evidence: backend/src/main/resources/application.yml:38-42
threats.mitigation: Require TLS on the JDBC URL and source credentials from a secret manager when the real datasource lands. Tracked together with TM-19.

diagrams.title: Level 1 — Login, lockout and session establishment

text.text: Server zone — Spring Security filter chain

data.name: Server zone — Spring Security filter chain
Browser (user agent)
data.description: Submits the login form as application/x-www-form-urlencoded.

data.name: CsrfFilter (CookieCsrfTokenRepository)
data.description: Validates X-XSRF-TOKEN against the XSRF-TOKEN cookie on every state-changing request.

threats.title: TM-38: No test asserts that a missing CSRF token is rejected
threats.description:
CSRF is correctly configured, but the 34 backend tests contain no case submitting a mutating request without X-XSRF-TOKEN and asserting 403. The control is therefore unverified and a future refactor could silently disable it — a regression that no build step would catch. Cookie attributes (HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite), CORS origin rejection and session-ID rotation on login are untested for the same reason.

Evidence: backend/src/test/java/... (no CSRF, CORS or cookie-attribute assertions in any of the 7 test classes)
threats.mitigation: Add integration tests: mutating call without the token → 403; with the token → success; a disallowed Origin → refused; assert the Set-Cookie attributes on login; assert the session id changes across authentication.

data.name: IpThrottleFilter
data.description: Runs before UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter; rejects throttled source IPs with 429 before any authentication attempt is made.

threats.title: TM-09: The IP throttle keys on getRemoteAddr(), so it is proxy-blind
threats.description:
Throttle state is keyed on request.getRemoteAddr() and no ForwardedHeaderFilter or server.forward-headers-strategy is configured. Behind any reverse proxy, load balancer or ingress — which is exactly how this would be deployed — every client collapses into a single key: the proxy's address. The consequences run both ways. Per-client throttling disappears entirely, so the PRD's requirement that IP throttling work independently of account lockout is not met in a real topology; and the tenth failed login from anyone locks out every user behind that proxy, turning a brute-force control into a whole-population denial of service.

Evidence: backend/.../auth/IpLoginThrottle.java:33, 40-70; backend/.../auth/LoginFailureHandler.java:75
threats.mitigation: Set server.forward-headers-strategy=framework and resolve the client IP from the trusted proxy's X-Forwarded-For, taking the rightmost untrusted hop rather than the leftmost (which is attacker-supplied). Pair it with an explicit list of trusted proxies so the header cannot be spoofed by a direct caller.

data.name: Form login → DaoAuthenticationProvider
data.description: loginProcessingUrl /api/auth/login. Loads the user through AppUserDetailsService, checks isAccountNonLocked()/isEnabled() before matching the BCrypt hash.

threats.title: Locked or disabled accounts still able to authenticate
threats.description: If lock and enabled state were checked after password matching, or not at all, a locked-out or suspended account could still obtain a session.
threats.mitigation: Mitigated: UserPrincipal computes isAccountNonLocked() from locked_until and isEnabled() from the enabled flag at load time, so DaoAuthenticationProvider throws LockedException/DisabledException before the password is even compared. Asserted by LockoutAndThrottlingTest.lockedAccountRejectsCorrectPasswordUntilCooldownExpires and AdminUserControllerTest's disable-then-cannot-login case.

data.name: LoginSuccessHandler

data.name: LoginFailureHandler
data.description: Increments the per-account counter, sets locked_until at the threshold, records the IP failure, returns a generic 401.

threats.title: TM-08: The failed-attempt counter never decays, enabling targeted account lockout
threats.description:
The PRD specifies N consecutive failures 'within a window'. There is no window: failed_login_attempts is a plain column incremented on every failure and reset only by a successful login. Five failures spread across months still lock the account. The practical consequence is an attacker who knows a username can lock that user out with five cheap requests, then repeat every 15 minutes indefinitely — the exact harm the PRD's separate IP-throttle clause was written to prevent, and it lands even when IP throttling works, because five attempts is under the ten-attempt IP threshold.

Evidence: backend/.../auth/LoginFailureHandler.java:84-95; backend/.../auth/LockoutPolicy.java:14-18; prd/assessment-prd.md:52
threats.mitigation: Record last_failed_login_at and treat the counter as expired once the window (e.g. 15 minutes) has elapsed since the last failure, so only genuinely consecutive failures within the window accumulate. Consider exponential backoff per account instead of a hard lock, so a legitimate user is delayed rather than denied.

data.name: IpLoginThrottle map (ConcurrentHashMap)
data.description: In-process map of remoteAddr → (failure count, window start). 10 failures / 15 min.

threats.title: TM-10: The throttle map has no eviction, so it grows without bound
threats.description:
Entries are added on every failed login from a new source address and removed only on a successful login from that same address. There is no TTL sweep, no size cap and no scheduled cleanup, so an attacker failing one login each from many spoofed or distributed source addresses grows the map indefinitely until the heap is exhausted. The control intended to blunt brute force is itself a memory-exhaustion vector.

Evidence: backend/.../auth/IpLoginThrottle.java:27-33, 40-70
threats.mitigation: Replace the hand-rolled map with a bounded, expiring cache (Caffeine with expireAfterWrite equal to the window and a maximumSize cap), or sweep expired windows on a scheduled task.

data.name: PasswordResetController
data.description: POST /api/auth/password-reset/request and /confirm. Both permitAll; request always answers 200 with the same generic message.

threats.title: TM-18b: Reset requests are unthrottled, so tokens can be minted without limit
threats.description:
IpThrottleFilter matches only POST /api/auth/login, so the reset-request endpoint accepts unlimited calls. Each call for a registered email writes a new token row and, once real email is wired up, sends a real message — so an attacker can flood a victim's inbox (a harassment and social-engineering vector that trains users to expect reset mails) and grow the token table without bound. Reset-confirm is likewise unthrottled, which matters less because the token space is 256 bits, but it costs a BCrypt hash per call.

Evidence: backend/.../auth/IpThrottleFilter.java:44-45; backend/.../passwordreset/PasswordResetController.java:23-27
threats.mitigation: Rate-limit both reset endpoints per source IP and per target email, and refuse to issue a new token while an unexpired one already exists for that user.

threats.title: TM-23: Response timing distinguishes registered from unregistered emails
threats.description:
The response body is identical either way, which is the guarantee the PRD asks for. The work behind it is not: an unregistered email returns after a single indexed lookup, while a registered one generates 32 random bytes, SHA-256 hashes them, writes a row inside a transaction, and calls the email service. The measurable difference is a side channel that recovers exactly the fact the uniform response was meant to hide.

Evidence: backend/.../passwordreset/PasswordResetService.java:75-94
threats.mitigation: Do the token work asynchronously so the response returns before it completes, or normalise the response time by performing equivalent dummy work on the miss path. Rate limiting (TM-18b) also raises the cost of collecting enough samples to average out noise.

threats.title: Account existence disclosed by the reset-request response
threats.description: A 404 or a differing message for an unknown email would expose which addresses hold accounts.
threats.mitigation: Mitigated: the controller returns the same 200 and message whether or not the email resolves, and the service simply returns early on a miss. Asserted by PasswordResetTest.requestReturnsGenericSuccessRegardlessOfWhetherEmailIsRegistered. The timing residual is TM-23.

data.name: PasswordResetService
data.description: Generates the token, stores only its SHA-256 hash with a 30-minute expiry, enforces single use, and expires every session for the user on success.

threats.title: Reset token guessing or forgery
threats.description: A predictable or short token would let an attacker forge a reset for an arbitrary account.
threats.mitigation: Mitigated: 32 bytes (256 bits) from SecureRandom, URL-safe Base64, stored only as a SHA-256 hash in a uniquely-indexed column, 30-minute expiry, single-use via used_at. Brute-forcing the space is infeasible and the database never holds a usable token. Asserted by PasswordResetTest.requestForRegisteredEmailIssuesASingleUseTokenHashOnly.

threats.title: Sessions surviving a password reset
threats.description: If existing sessions stayed valid after a reset, a user resetting a password precisely because they suspect compromise would leave the attacker logged in.
threats.mitigation: Mitigated: invalidateAllSessionsFor() walks SessionRegistry and calls expireNow() on every session belonging to the user; RestSessionExpiredStrategy then answers 401. Asserted by PasswordResetTest.confirmWithValidTokenUpdatesPasswordMarksTokenUsedAndInvalidatesSessions. Constrained to one instance — see TM-25.

threats.title: Token reuse or use after expiry
threats.description: A replayable or indefinitely valid token extends a single interception into lasting account access.
threats.mitigation: Mitigated: confirmReset rejects a token whose used_at is set or whose expires_at has passed, and marks it used inside the same transaction. Both paths asserted by PasswordResetTest (confirmWithAlreadyUsedTokenIsRejected, confirmWithExpiredTokenIsRejected).

data.name: EmailService (stub)
data.description: Out of scope for delivery per the PRD; logs the link instead of sending it. The logging behaviour is in scope — see TM-02.

data.name: password_reset_tokens
data.description: user_id, token_hash (unique), expires_at, used_at.

threats.title: TM-18: Superseded tokens stay valid and spent tokens are never purged
threats.description:
Issuing a new reset token does not invalidate the user's existing unexpired ones, so several valid tokens can coexist for one account — a user who requests a reset twice because the first mail was slow leaves two live paths into the account, and an attacker who intercepted an earlier one keeps it. Separately, expired and used rows are never deleted: the table only grows, and it retains a permanent, timestamped record of every reset attempt per user.

Evidence: backend/.../passwordreset/PasswordResetService.java:83-86; PasswordResetTokenRepository.java:11-13
threats.mitigation: Invalidate all outstanding tokens for the user when a new one is issued, and add a scheduled job deleting rows past expiry plus a retention bound.

diagrams.title: Level 1 — Admin user management and bootstrap

data.name: AdminUserList (React)
data.description: Rendered only when role === 'ADMIN' and disables self-targeting buttons — both cosmetic.

threats.title: Client-side admin gating relied on for security
threats.description: A user who edits client state or calls the API directly bypasses any UI-level gating.
threats.mitigation: Mitigated: the UI checks are cosmetic by design and the server is authoritative — hasRole('ADMIN') on /api/admin/**, and the self-action guard lives in the service using the authenticated principal's id. AdminUserControllerTest asserts a USER gets 403 on every mutation and 401 when unauthenticated.

data.name: Spring Security URL authorization
data.description: requestMatchers("/api/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN") — the sole authorization check. See TM-14.

data.name: AdminUserController
data.description: Passes @AuthenticationPrincipal UserPrincipal's id as the acting admin; never reads identity from the body.

data.name: AdminUserManagementService
data.description: setEnabled / changeRole / delete, each guarded by requireNotSelf(actingAdminId, targetUserId).

threats.title: TM-04: Disabling or demoting a user does not revoke their live session
threats.description:
setEnabled(false) and changeRole(USER) write the users row and nothing else — neither touches SessionRegistry. Authority is evaluated at authentication time and cached in the session's Authentication, so a user who is already logged in keeps their old privileges until the session expires (up to the container's implicit 30-minute idle default, indefinitely if they stay active). An admin suspending a compromised or departing account believes access is cut; it is not. A demoted admin retains admin authorities and can re-promote themselves before the session lapses, which defeats the revocation entirely. The same codebase already solves this for password reset via PasswordResetService.invalidateAllSessionsFor(), so the capability exists and is simply not called here — an inconsistent revocation story rather than a missing mechanism.

Evidence: backend/.../admin/AdminUserManagementService.java:42-67; backend/.../passwordreset/PasswordResetService.java:130, 135-143
threats.mitigation: Call the same SessionRegistry expiry logic from setEnabled(false), changeRole and delete. Extract it into a shared SessionRevoker collaborator so there is one implementation, and add tests asserting a disabled or demoted user's existing session is rejected on its next request.

threats.title: TM-17: Nothing protects the last remaining admin account
threats.description:
The only guard is 'not yourself'. With two admins, either can disable, demote or delete the other, leaving one admin; that survivor cannot act on themselves, so a single mistake or one compromised admin account can leave the system with no usable administrator. Recovery means direct database edits — precisely what the PRD's bootstrap story exists to avoid — and AdminBootstrapRunner will not help, because it seeds only when no ADMIN row exists at all, and a disabled ADMIN row still counts as existing.

Evidence: backend/.../admin/AdminUserManagementService.java:43, 57, 71, 88-92; backend/.../user/AdminBootstrapRunner.java:42-57
threats.mitigation: Reject any mutation that would leave zero enabled ADMIN accounts, and treat a disabled admin as absent for the purposes of the bootstrap check (or seed on 'no enabled admin' rather than 'no admin').

threats.title: An admin locking themselves out or escalating via self-targeting
threats.description: An admin disabling, demoting or deleting their own account would strand themselves and could be used to manipulate privilege state.
threats.mitigation: Mitigated: requireNotSelf compares the target id against the authenticated principal's id on all three mutations and throws SelfActionNotAllowedException → 400. All three cases asserted by AdminUserControllerTest. The gap is the collective case, TM-17.

threats.title: TM-39: Destructive admin actions lack an accountable audit trail
threats.description:
Deleting a user is irreversible and removes their reset tokens too, yet the only record is an unstructured INFO line carrying actor id and target username — no client IP, no correlation id, no immutable audit store, and no re-authentication or confirmation step in front of the action.

Evidence: backend/.../admin/AdminUserManagementService.java:49-50, 63-64, 81-85
threats.mitigation: Require step-up re-authentication for delete, write admin mutations to an append-only audit table (actor, target, action, source IP, timestamp) in the same transaction, and consider soft-delete so the action is recoverable. Overlaps TM-27.

data.name: AdminBootstrapRunner
data.description: On startup, seeds one ADMIN from app.admin.username/password if no ADMIN row exists.

threats.title: Predictable initial admin credentials shipping to a real deployment
threats.description: A hardcoded default admin password is the classic path into a freshly deployed system.
threats.mitigation: Mitigated in the base profile: app.admin.username and app.admin.password bind to ${APP_ADMIN_USERNAME} and ${APP_ADMIN_PASSWORD} with no defaults, so startup fails rather than seeding a guessable account, and the seeded password is BCrypt-hashed like any other. The dev profile's defaults are the live problem — TM-07.

Data subject (registered user)
data.description: Supplies a username, an email address and a password at registration.

threats.title: TM-30: No privacy notice, lawful basis record or consent moment
threats.description:
Registration collects an email address and stores it indefinitely, but nothing tells the user what it is for, how long it is kept, or who can see it. The PRD states email is used only for password reset; the user is never shown that. There is no notice, no consent interaction, and no documented lawful basis.

Evidence: frontend/src/RegistrationForm.tsx; no privacy notice anywhere in the repo
threats.mitigation: Add a short privacy notice at the point of collection stating the purpose (password reset only), the retention period, and who can access it. Record the lawful basis as an ADR.

threats.title: TM-31: No retention policy, erasure path or data-subject access route
threats.description:
Nothing in the system bounds how long personal data is kept. The users table retains every account forever unless an admin deletes it; password_reset_tokens accumulates a permanent timestamped history of reset attempts (TM-18); logs have no retention configuration at all (TM-27). There is no self-service erasure, export or rectification path — deletion is admin-only, so a data subject cannot exercise erasure or access rights without a human intermediary. Under PDPA/GDPR-style regimes that is a compliance gap, not just a feature gap.

Evidence: prd/assessment-prd.md (no retention requirement); backend/.../admin/AdminUserManagementService.java:71-86
threats.mitigation: Define and implement retention periods for accounts, reset tokens and logs; add a self-service account deletion and data-export endpoint; document the retention schedule alongside the lawful basis.

threats.title: TM-32: Account existence is externally probeable, identifying account holders
threats.description:
The 409 conflict on registration confirms whether a given username or email belongs to an account (TM-22). Anyone holding a list of email addresses can learn which of those people use this system — a membership disclosure about identified individuals, independent of whether they can log in.

Evidence: backend/.../auth/RegistrationService.java:45-52
threats.mitigation: Same remediation as TM-22: make the registration response uniform and signal the conflict out of band.

threats.title: TM-33: Timing reveals whether an email address is registered
threats.description:
The uniform response body hides account existence; the response time does not (TM-23). An observer can detect the presence of a data subject's record without ever authenticating.

Evidence: backend/.../passwordreset/PasswordResetService.java:75-94
threats.mitigation: Equalise the work on both paths or move token issuance off the request thread; rate-limit to raise the sampling cost.

threats.title: TM-34: Every admin can read every user's email address
threats.description:
GET /api/admin/users returns the full email address of every registered user to any ADMIN, in one call, with no field-level minimisation, no purpose limitation and no access logging on the read. The PRD's own data model says email exists solely to support password reset — bulk admin visibility serves no stated purpose, and a single compromised admin session exfiltrates the entire address book.

Evidence: backend/.../admin/AdminUserController.java; backend/.../admin/UserSummaryResponse.java
threats.mitigation: Drop email from the default listing and expose it only on an explicit per-user lookup that is purpose-logged, or mask it (j***@example.com). Log admin reads of personal data, not just mutations.

data.name: users (username, email)
data.description: Directly identifying personal data, retained indefinitely.

threats.title: TM-35: Username, email and behaviour are linkable with no separation
threats.description: The users row ties a username to an email address permanently, and log lines tie that same username to login times, failure patterns and source-address-derived throttling state (TM-27). Nothing separates identifiers by context or bounds how long the linkage persists, so an operator with log access can build a behavioural profile of an identified individual from data collected for authentication.
threats.mitigation: Log a stable pseudonymous user id rather than the username, keep the id-to-username mapping in one place, and bound log retention.

threats.title: TM-36: Personal data and reset secrets land in logs with no retention bound
threats.description:
The logged reset link contains both the data subject's email address and a live account-takeover token (TM-02, TM-03), and usernames appear across the audit lines. Logs go to stdout with no retention, access control, redaction or shipping policy, so personal data spreads to wherever stdout is collected — CI output, terminal scrollback, container log drivers, aggregators — and stays there indefinitely.

Evidence: backend/.../passwordreset/EmailService.java:16-18
threats.mitigation: Stop logging the link and the email (log a correlation id and pseudonymous user id instead), then define retention, access control and redaction for whatever remains.

threats.title: TM-37: Authentication events are recorded permanently with no purpose or retention limit
threats.description: Login successes, failures and lockouts are logged per username and kept forever. Accountability is the point, so this is a deliberate trade-off — but with no retention limit the record outlives its security purpose and becomes a permanent activity history the data subject cannot see, correct or expire.
threats.mitigation: Bound retention to the period needed for security investigation and state that period in the privacy notice.
